full_judgment:
2. The circumstances giving rise to this application briefly stated are as follow: The detenue is the 6th daughter of the petitioner, Prafulla Kamal Bhattacharya who claims her to be a minor having been born on 13-6-63. She was a student of Class-VIII of Elenga Girls High School in September last. On the 12th September, 1975 she went to School as usual but did not return home in the evening whereupon the petitioner went to the School and learnt that his daughter had been taken to Tangail by an ex-student, named Raushan Ara, on the plea of witnessing a cinema show there but the said Roushan Ara handed her over to one Rahmat Ali Talukder. Rahmat Ali Talukder, it was further learn forcibly took the girl into a truck and started for Mymensingh. The petitioner immediately went to the Kalihati Police Station and lodged a First Information Report alleging these facts whereupon the police registered a case under section 366 of the Penal Code against Rahmat Ali Talukder and others and on 1-9-75 recovered the girl from the custody of said Rahmat Ali. The police, on the following day i.e. 2-9-75 produced both the girl and accused Rahrnat Ali Talukder before the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Tangail with recommendation that both the persons should be detained in custody till the investigation of the case. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate accordingly sent them into custody refusing their prayer for bail Accused Rahmat Ali, however, denied the allegation made against him and contended that the girl was Major and of her own accord married him. In support of this contention Rahmat Ali filed a Medical Certificate from a Radiologist endorsed by the Civil Surgeon, Tangail which showed that the age of the girl was between 18-19 years. The detenue also made a statement before the Magistrate supporting the contention of Rahmat Ali. Petitioner challenged the opinion of the Radiologist as to the age of the girl and produced a Passport, a School Certificate, a Horoscope and a Declaration made by him at the border check-post while he had entered with his family into India in 1971. These papers supported his claim that his daughter was aged about 13 years. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate heard both the parties again on 10-9-75, examined the documents as to age of the girl submitted by the contending parties and, by his order of the same date, granted bail to the detenue allowing her to go where ever she liked. The petitioner immediately challenged this order of the. Magistrate before the Sessions judge Tangail, by a revisional application and obtained "stay" of the order. Thereafter, the petitioner made this. application u/s 491 Cr. P.C. and obtained this Rule; on his prayer the detenue was transferred from the Tangail Sub-jail to the Central Jail, Dacca on the ground that she was not free from outside influences, in the Tangail Sub-Jail. 

 3. None of the four opposite parties who are Government Officials; such as the Secretary, Home Affairs, Govt. of Bangladesh the Deputy Commissioner and the Sub-Divisional Officer, Tangail and the Jailor appeared in this case. But the detenue appeared through a lawyer of his Court namely Mr. Shah Azizur Rahman to contest this application on certain points. 

 5. The main question, namely, the only question for determination in this case is the age of the detenue. For, if the girl is minor the person best entitled to her custody will be her father; the petitioner. But the interest of the girl herself will also to be taken into consideration in the light of the Guardian and Wards Act, 1887. On the other hand, if the girl is major, being aged 16 years or over, her will, in the circumstances as disclosed above, must prevail and since she is not an accused in the Police Case as referred to, she cannot be detained against her will. On this view we are supported by uniform decisions of this court given in a great number of cases, such as "Miss Purna Chowdhury Vs. State", 3 DLR, 293; "Ayesha Begum & Jotsna Vs. State", 15 DLR (Dacca), 148; "Santipad Ganguli Vs. Sova Rani Ganguli", (Cr. Revision Case No. 360 of 1959, unreported); "Nittananda Dutta Vs. Ashraf Ali", (Cr. Revision Case No. 778 of 1961-unreported), and "Ramesh Chandra Mandai Vs. Atiqullah", (Cr. Misc. Case No. 59 of 1961- unreported). 

 7. The petitioner in support of his statement as to age of the detenue submitted a Horroscope. The Horroscope supports his statement as to the age of the detenue. But a Horroscope is no like a birth-register which is maintained, under some provisions of law, at any office, such as the Municipality, entries wherein are made in normal course of business. This horoscope is a loose-sheet of paper and as such, the possibility of preparing a Horroscope for the purpose of a case is always there. The petitioner submitted a School Certificate issued by the Headmistress of the Elenga Girls High School in which the detenue had been reading at the relevant time. This certificate shows that according to the School Admission Register the date of her birth is 13-3-63 i.e. it agrees with the statement of the petitioner. This entry as to age of the girl was made long before the present incident and as such it has been contended, its authenticity cannot be questioned. But age of students as entered in School Admission Register is sometimes understated. However, in this case the detenue was a student of Class VIII in September, 1975 and her age, according to the Admission Register, was a little less than 13 years; she was aged about 5 years when she got her first admission in School in the Infant Class or Class-I. If she is 19 years now according to the report of the Medical Board, then she was about 12 years when she had got her first admission in School in the Infant Class or Class I. It is, rather improbable that a girl of about 11/12 years age would seek admission in the Infant Class and even if she had taken admission at that age it was unlikely that her age would be understated by about 6 years. The age of the girl as shown in the School Certificate fits in the circumstances as found above. 

 (Other data in respect of a female, as referred to, include general configuration, height and weight, eruption of teeth, growth of hair, development of breasts, changes in the external genitals, establishment of menstruation, and ossification and union of bones. The report of the Medical Board has not specifically referred to these data. Modi in his "Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology", (14th edition at page 31) has observed as to Ossification of bones as "This sign is helpful for determining age until ossification is completed, for Skiagraph has now made it possible to determine even in living persons the extent of ossification and the union of epiphyses in bones. Owing to the variations in climatic, dietetic, hereditary and other factors affecting the people of the different states of India it cannot be reasonably expected to formulate a uniform standard for the determination of the age of the union of epiphysis for the whole of India. In ascertaining the age of young person's radiograms of any of the main joints of the upper or the lower extremity of both sides of the body should be taken, and an opinion should be given according to the following table, but it must be remembered that too much reliance should not be placed on this table as it merely indicates an average and is likely to vary in individual cases even of the same province owing to the eccentricities of development." 

 This view was relied upon in a number of cases which have been cited here by Mr. Shawkat Ali Khan such as--Emperor Vs. Kudrat, A.I.R. 1939 All 708, Zaitoon Begum Vs, Emperor. A.I.R. 1956 Sind 13 and Mora Debi vs. State of Kerala A.I.R. 1958, Kerala 8. In the last mentioned case it has been observed that the medical evidence as to age of a person cannot be utilised to override the effect of other cogent evidence on the point. 

 12. The next case relied upon by Mr. Shawkat Ali Khan is Chatu vs. Gabindam Kutty, A.I.R. 1958, Kerala, 121. In that case the age of a girl taken away from her father's custody was examined and a Division Bench of that High Court rejected the opinion of a Radiologist who put the age of the girl at 19 years by ossification test According to the evidence of the father of the girl, supported by School admission Register and Birth Register, her age was 17 years 5 months. The Division Bench presided over by Koshi C.J. rejected the opinion of the Radiologist and preferred the other evidence on the point, observing as follows:- 

 Modi's observation in his Medical Jurisprudence as already quoted by us above was also referred to in that case. 

 13. The next Case cited by Mr. Shawkat Ali Khan is "Deba Prasad Bose Vs. The King", 54 C.W.N. 32.9 decided by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court which did not accept the report of a Radiologist regarding the age a girl in view of other evidence on the point and observed that due to variation in different factors affecting the people of different states of India uniform results of ossification tests could not be expected. The other cases cited by Mr. Shawkat Ali Khan on this point are "Golam Kadri VS. Noor Mohammad", 6 D.L.R. (\V.P.), 178, "Viamikba vs. State", 18 D.L.R. (W.P.), 18; "Md. Nasim Vs. Crown", P.L.D. 1957 Lahore, 109; and "Sabir Hussain Vs. State," 21 D.L.R. (W.P.), 5. We need not refer to these cases individually since the experts opinions given in those Cases were not from Radiologists but from other experts, such as medical 'men and handwriting experts. The principle followed in those cases, are, however the same, that is, in the face of other cogent evidence, the opinion of an expert could be rejected by the Court. 

 15. In the light of the opinions expressed in the cases cited above and in view of the medico-legal opinion that a Radiologist's examination indicates the approximate age of the person examined, his opinion may be accepted subject to variation by two or three years. In the case of a person having quick physical growth such variation is very much likely. The petitioner's statement has been corroborated by at-least three official documents, the School Certificate the Passport and the Declaration. Entries as to age of the detenue in these documents having been made long before the incident in question, they can be reasonably expected to be true. But in view of the wide divergence between the age as indicated by the Medical Board and that appearing from the other evidence we directed- that the detenue should be produced before us. Accordingly she was produced before us 'in Court on 19-1-76. We have seen her, but her appearance she does not show her to be 19 years old. The age as given by the Medical Board does not fit in her appearance, She looks very tender-aged, and though it is not possible for us to determine her exact age from her appearance, we think that her age could not be 16 years. To us she appears to be aged below 16 years, and as such she is minor. But when we asked her whether she is willing to return to her father's custody she refused. But the minor's refusal is not material so far her custody is concerned. The father is certainly the best well-wisher of his daughter and in her own interest she should go into her father's custody. In the case "Kiron Bala Chowdhury Vs. State", 17 D.L.R., Dacca, 544, a Division Bench of this Court directed that the detenue who was a minor girl should be made over to the custody of her mother since she should not be left in the street.
